Qualification · Employer guide · Draft

Certified versus qualified: what’s the difference?

Certification is an important credential. It is one part of the employer’s responsibility to prepare and evaluate an operator.

The short answer

Certification and employer evaluation serve different purposes. For cranes covered by OSHA’s construction rule, employers must address training, certification or licensing, and evaluation before assigning an operator, subject to the rule’s exceptions and operator-in-training provisions.

A credential is a checkpoint

Certification assesses knowledge and practical skills through a defined testing process. It does not remove the employer’s duty to evaluate an operator for the equipment and work the employer assigns.

Keep the three pieces visible

  • Training: prepare the employee for the knowledge and skills the role requires.
  • Certification or licensing: confirm the applicable credential requirements and their scope.
  • Employer evaluation: establish and document the operator’s ability for the assigned equipment and activities.

What should a supervisor ask?

Before making an assignment, review what the employee has learned, what has been observed in practice, what the evaluation covers, and which gaps remain. A course completion record should never be treated as permission to operate.

Keep the scope visible in the record: equipment, tasks, evaluator, date, and follow-up needs. The employer remains responsible for qualification and work authorization.

Where does CraneQualified fit?

CraneQualified supports structured development and competency documentation. That evidence helps the employer see readiness gaps and make informed decisions; it does not transfer the employer’s responsibilities to a course or platform.

Check the rule for your work

This draft addresses U.S. construction cranes. Other equipment, industries, and jurisdictions may have different requirements. Review the applicable rule and your operating conditions before assigning work.

Sample / draft article. Prepared for this website preview; editorial and technical review are required before public publication. This is general development guidance, not a determination that a particular person is qualified or authorized.

Regulatory reference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1427 — Operator training, certification, and evaluation. Source reviewed October 12, 2026.
